Incriminate

in-KRIM-uh-nayt -- from Latin in- ('into') + criminare ('to accuse'), from crimen ('crime, accusation'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To incriminate to point to or strongly imply someone's guilt in a crime or wrongdoing.

The security footage clearly seemed to incriminate the night-shift cashier, though he insisted he was innocent.

Worked Example

Detectives found a receipt in the suspect's jacket that placed him at the exact store, at the exact time, that would go on to incriminate him more than any witness testimony.

That piece of evidence pointing directly toward someone's guilt -- even without a confession -- is exactly what it means to incriminate someone.

How Incriminate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

implicate

implicate: to show that someone is connected to a wrongdoing

accuse

accuse: to formally charge someone with an offense

Antonyms

exculpate

exculpate: to show that someone is not guilty of a crime

absolve

absolve: to free someone from blame or guilt

How Strong Is It? — implicate → accuse → incriminate

implicate vs. incriminate

implicate vs. incriminate: The testimony implicated two other employees who had helped cover up the theft.

accuse vs. incriminate

accuse vs. incriminate: The neighbor publicly accused the landlord of ignoring the building's broken heating system.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: into (Latin)

root — crimin-

root — crimin-: accusation, crime (Latin (crimen))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin in- ('into') plus crimen ('accusation, crime') plus the verb suffix -ate. To incriminate someone is literally to draw them into an accusation of crime.

Use the root in a new word: discriminate
